label: TMUA early specimen · Paper 2 · Question 20

hints.title: Use the strongest statements first
hints.body: Q says both women’s statements are true; T says neither is true. Those assertions cannot both be true. Separate Q true, T true, and both false.
hints.recap: Three cases cover Q and T.
hints.pitfall: Q and T are not logical negations: both can be false if exactly one woman’s statement is true.
hints.pause: Write the consequences for S in each case.

recall.reminder: Split into exhaustive cases rather than assuming only the extremes are possible.

hints.title: Keep the implication inside R
hints.body: If R is true, P is true as well, because R asserts both a name fact and P’s truth. A false R does not force P false: the name fact may fail.
hints.recap: R implies P, but the converse is unavailable.
hints.pitfall: Do not assume whether R’s first name really is Robert.
hints.pause: Use <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>⇒</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> to test S’s claim that exactly one man speaks truth.

recall.reminder: AND requires both parts; its failure need not make both parts false.

hints.title: Check P against the final count
hints.body: P’s statement must agree with the parity of the total number of true statements. A provisional assignment is valid only if every statement, including this count statement, matches.
hints.pitfall: Counting a tentative table is not enough if P’s own claim then becomes false.
hints.pause: Finish the three cases and record all attainable truth counts.

recall.reminder: Combine conditions before choosing, and check consistency of the resulting truth assignment.

solution:
Let P,Q,R,S,T denote the truth values of the five statements. R true implies P true, but R false may simply mean that the name assertion is false. Q and T cannot both be true.

Q true, T false: Q forces S true. Then exactly one man must be truthful. Since T is false and R would force P, the only possibility is P true and R false. P,Q,S are the three truths, consistent with P’s odd-count claim. This is attainable when R’s first name is not Robert.

Q false, T true: both women are false. S false means the number of truthful men is not one. T is already true, so at least one of P,R is true; R implies P, so P is true. P then requires an odd total, forcing R true too. P,R,T are the three truths. This is attainable when R’s first name is Robert.

Q and T both false: T false means at least one woman is true; with Q false, S must be true. Exactly one man is true, so P is true and R false. But then only P and S are true, a total of two, contradicting P. This case is impossible.

Every consistent case has exactly three true statements.

Answer D: 3 only.
knowledgePattern: Truth consistency with self-reference and unknown factual atom
